prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are probed without perturbation from the trap, bringing optical frequency standards to a fractional uncertainty of 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep B007 as a single-part prize with Katori and Ye, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. After the second reading I would put the case on four points. First, the physical idea is simple and original: choosing the lattice wavelength so that the light shift is the same for both clock states removes the perturbation that had kept trapped neutral atoms from precision spectroscopy. Second, the idea reached its promise in experiment: many atoms interrogated together give a statistical advantage that single-ion clocks cannot match, and the many-body systematics work, such as collisional and tunnelling shifts, is real physics in its own right and not only engineering. Third, the check I always ask for is met: JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL reach comparable performance, and comparisons across fibre links agree. Fourth, the results already give something about nature, namely resolution of the gravitational redshift over millimetre to centimetre height differences and tighter limits on drifting constants and some dark-matter couplings. As a theorist who works with superconducting qubits, I know what it takes to make a quantum system coherent enough to measure something with it. A lattice clock does this for an ensemble at the 1e-18 level, and I see that as a clear quantum-physics achievement. In answer to the chair's question on the citation, I would word the novelty as a property of the scheme, not of accuracy alone: the magic-wavelength lattice, which makes a many-atom, trap-free optical clock possible. That separates it from the 2005 comb prize, which gave a way to count optical cycles, and from the 2012 ion-control prize, which gave control of one quantum system at a time. On timing, I take a position and do not just list the risk. We should not wait for the redefinition of the second. That decision belongs to the metrology bodies. The demonstrated and independently compared performance is what the committee has to judge.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is that a sceptic can still read lattice clocks as the third prize in one metrology line (2005, 2012, now 2026), and that the prize would reward an instrument and its accuracy more than a discovery about nature. I do not agree, for the reasons given above, but I accept that the committee has to say it in the citation and not assume it. The second objection is attribution at the edges. Lemonde, Derevianko and Pal'chikov, and the ion-clock groups, made contributions that a two-name credit leaves out, and I cannot settle the 2001-2003 priority from memory. I rely on Lindroth, Kroll and Olsson to check the record, and if that check showed that Katori's proposal was not independent and primary, I would reopen the credit. The third objection is that B007 reached its majority partly because members read each other's opening ballots. That is true of my own move from B044, and the final ballot should rest on each member's scientific judgment and not on the count.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B007 from B012 after the opening, but says that if the committee wants a discovery about nature rather than an instrument, B012 is his stronger candidate and should not be lost. He also says AMO and metrology are outside his expertise and relies on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson for the B007 physics.
responses.response: I take that reliance seriously. On the physics I can say that the magic-wavelength condition is not a refinement of earlier ion-clock work but a different way to get stability, by interrogating many atoms without perturbation from the trap. I also see his point on discovery against instrument. B007 does give a measurement of something in nature, namely the gravitational redshift over centimetre scales and the limits on drifting constants, so I read it as both. I do not think B012 should be lost, and that is why I list it as my first alternative this time. But I stay with my round-1 view that two names for IceCube is a bigger attribution risk than two names for clocks, and I would need an answer to that before ranking B012 above B007.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps B012 first with Halzen and Karle, calls the diffuse flux a clue from nature, and says plainly that a prize only two of eight members rank cannot be sustained by his enthusiasm. He asks whether the committee should accept the clearest-attribution, broadest-support option (B007) over a stronger discovery case.
responses.response: I respect that candour. My answer is that I am not choosing B007 because of the count. I judge the physical case to be at least as strong as the astroparticle case for a prize this year, because B007 has a reproduced result at the stated precision and a named credit I can defend publicly. I cannot judge the IceCube priority record, and I defer to him on whether Halzen and Karle alone is defensible. He has not yet said how he would treat the AMANDA and Baikal precursors in a citation. If he can show that the credit is clean and that the NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane results do not carry the weight, I would move B012 up as a second part, but that would leave a one-name seat only under the three-person limit and he has not proposed that.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B032 first on scientific grounds, since exact fluctuation relations tested over thirty years are model-independent. She concedes that attribution among Evans, Cohen, Morriss, Searles, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert cannot be resolved in three names, and lists B007 as her first alternative. She asks whether theorems confirmed by experiment count as a discovery.
responses.response: I think her question about confirmation against discovery is the right one, and I would answer that a prize for B032 is possible in principle because the relations were tested in single-molecule and single-electron experiments. But that testing confirmed what the theorems predicted, and the priority problem she describes is exactly the kind that would make the citation contested. I admit that I judge B032 from the edge of my own field, so I would defer to her on the physics. I would ask her this: if the committee could not resolve the credit within three names, would she accept B007 as the prize, as her listing of it as first alternative suggests? I read her file as saying that she would.

responses.point: Lindroth explains the magic-wavelength condition as simple atomic physics, notes that Katori proposed it and demonstrated early strontium lattice clocks, and asks whether a second part would be needed. She names B041 and B043 as candidates for a second achievement and flags the Chu overlap for B043.
responses.response: I agree with her description of the physical heart of the prize, and I accept that her reading of the credit (Katori for the idea and first lattice clocks, Ye for accuracy and many-atom systematics) is the right one for the citation. On a second part, I do not think the committee has a candidate with a settled interpretation and a credit of one more name. B043 has the Chu overlap she raises and B041 needs four names. I would therefore keep to a single part. I would ask her, as one of the AMO members, to say clearly whether she has now checked the 2001-2003 priority record, because the chair's question on that is the one that could still change my credit.

responses.point: Olsson says she can check the first-demonstration question against the record. She notes that credit for the first lattice demonstration and for the record accuracy is claimed in different ways by Katori's and Ye's groups, and that Lemonde and Pal'chikov on the magic-wavelength ideas lie outside the credit.
responses.response: This is the point I most want her to settle. If the record shows that Katori proposed and first demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice with strontium in 2001-2003, and that Ye's contribution was the accuracy and stability frontier, then the split of credit in my citation is correct and I need not add names. If it shows that the proposal was shared in a way that makes Katori's primary credit contestable, I would want to reopen the credit. I also note her disclosure of a University of Tokyo connection. I see it as a reason to disclose but not as a reason for her to step back, since she has no collaboration with Katori.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B007 from B018 but says he feels the pull of condensed-matter candidates, such as DMFT and magic-angle graphene, and does not want a strong metrology case to crowd out condensed matter because it has the broadest opening support. He lists the open pairing mechanism and sample dependence in B005.
responses.response: I think his caution about letting the count decide is right, and I share it. I am also an outsider on B018 and B005, so I rely on his view of maturity. On B005 I agree that the open pairing mechanism is a real obstacle for this year, and that is why it stays as my second alternative and not as a preferred part. If he wants either as a second part, he should propose a credit of one extra name, since Katori and Ye already take two of the three places. I do not see how B018 or B005 can fit that limit now.

uncertainties: Exact priority between Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice demonstrations, the parallel suggestions of Lemonde, Derevianko and Pal'chikov, and Ye's work. I rely on recollection and want AMO members to confirm it.
Whether the committee will accept the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether my proposed wording in the citation is enough.
Whether the neutral-atom lattice clock has an edge over the best ion clocks in accuracy that the citation should state, or only in stability, since both reach comparable accuracy.
Whether IceCube (B012) can be given a clean two- or three-name credit; I cannot judge this and defer to Danielsson and Pearce.
Whether a single-part prize is right this year, since I have not seen a second part with a settled interpretation and a credit of at most one additional name.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I am director of WACQT and work in the same superconducting-circuit community as the B044 candidates, with long-standing Chalmers collaborations with experimental groups there, so I should not weigh B044 as an impartial member. I no longer list it as a preferred part or an alternative in this round so as to avoid any appearance of influence. Kroll shares WACQT management with me, and I would recuse from any discussion in which B044 became a serious option. I have no personal or institutional link to Katori, Ye or the other B007 names, nor to B012 or B005 as far as I know.
